episodes.title: Odyssey CEO Oliver Cameron is 90% sure we live in a simulation | E2358
episodes.about: Odyssey co-founder and CEO Oliver Cameron builds simulated worlds for a living. His team dropped a simulated fruit fly brain into an AI world that is being rendered and created in real time, and 6.2 million people have watched the virtual fly navigate an imaginary world on X. The conversation digs into how world models learn about physics, gravity, and causality just by watching videos, what makes Odyssey-3 an ideal training ground for AI agents, and why a world model only renders the parts of the world that are currently being experienced.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — This Week in Startups is Jason Calacanis's startup interview show, new here: Odyssey put a simulated fruit fly brain inside a world model rendered in real time, and Cameron explains how models learn physics and causality from watching video.

episodes.title: The $1,000 Hack That Turns Everyday Cars Hands-Free
episodes.about: Aftermarket devices promise to turn some recent model cars into hands-free vehicles. WSJ reporter Christopher Otts explains how these kits work, what it's like to ride with one, and the growing safety, regulatory, and industry questions surrounding third-party driver-assistance tech. Julie Chang hosts.
episodes.why: Out today, 12 minutes: a $1,000 aftermarket kit turns an ordinary recent car hands-free, and the WSJ rode with one and pressed on the safety and regulatory questions that follow.

episodes.title: How to Deslopify Your AI
episodes.about: AI slop shifts the burden of thinking from the person producing the work to whoever receives it. In this Operators' Cut, Nufar Gaspar joins NLW to share practical habits for creating better work with AI, from developing your own point of view and teaching models your taste to building effective review checkpoints. NLW also breaks down how he uses AI to produce How We Got Here while keeping control of its perspective and narrative.
episodes.why: NLW and Nufar Gaspar on deslopifying: slop pushes the thinking onto whoever receives the work, and the counter is a point of view of your own, models taught your taste, and real review checkpoints.

episodes.title: The Robots Already Working in American Factories | Tutor Intelligence
episodes.about: What does it take to build robots that can actually work in factories and warehouses? Tutor Intelligence CEO Josh Gruenstein argues robotics is a systems problem spanning AI, hardware, manufacturing, and the work itself. Josh joins a16z General Partners Martin Casado and Raghu Raghuram to explain Tutor's approach: deploy robots into real businesses, use human 'tutors' when needed, and turn that work into training data that makes the robots more capable. They discuss Tutor's 100-robot data factory, robots starting at roughly $16 an hour, advances in spatial reasoning, and what flexible robotic labor could mean for American manufacturing and the physical economy.
episodes.why: Tutor Intelligence already runs 100 robots in real factories at roughly $16 an hour: humans tutor them through the hard parts, and every shift becomes training data.

episodes.title: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
episodes.about: Legora can't read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm's clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can't see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora.
episodes.why: The hard version of building agents: Legora's legal agents work on client data the company's own engineers are never allowed to see, so Lauritzen has to build and test them without reading a single trace.
